steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar Component  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose (lacking an oxygen on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA contains ribose (with a hydroxyl group on the 2′ carbon).

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), uracil (U) in place of thymine, cytosine (C), and guanine (G).

3. Strandedness  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes.

4. Function  
   • DNA stores and transmits genetic information across generations.  
   • RNA plays multiple roles in gene expression and regulation:  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA) carries coding instructions from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA) helps assemble amino acids into proteins.  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA) is a structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.  
     – Other noncoding RNAs regulate gene expression, RNA processing, and defense.

5. Location in the Cell  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA resides mainly in the nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions both there and in the cytoplasm.

6. Stability  
   • DNA is chemically more stable (ideal for long-term storage) due to its deoxyribose sugar and double-stranded form.  
   • RNA is less stable (more prone to hydrolysis) because of the 2′-OH group and single strand, making it suitable for transient roles.

7. Molecular Size  
   • Genomic DNA molecules are very large (millions of base pairs).  
   • RNA molecules are shorter (typically a few hundred to a few thousand nucleotides, though rRNAs and some lncRNAs can be longer).

Summary  
DNA is the long-term, double-stranded genetic blueprint built on deoxyribose and using thymine, whereas RNA is a more versatile, shorter, usually single-stranded molecule built on ribose and using uracil, with diverse roles in translating and regulating that genetic information.
